plan.topic_summary: High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) is a 3D-stacked DRAM architecture that delivers extreme memory bandwidth for AI accelerators and high-performance computing. For a 1–5 year view, the key question is how successive HBM generations evolve in capacity, interconnect technology, and cost, and how these dynamics reshape the competitive structure of the AI hardware supply chain.
key_questions: What is the current supply-demand balance for HBM3E, and how are capacity constraints affecting pricing and allocation across AI accelerator customers?
What are the yield rates and cost structures for current-generation HBM, and how do they compare to prior generations in terms of cost per bit?
How will the transition to HBM4 and hybrid bonding affect the competitive positioning of memory suppliers and the packaging/foundry ecosystem over the next 1–3 years?
What are the thermal and power limits of next-generation HBM stacks, and how do they constrain AI accelerator design and datacenter power budgets?
Could emerging alternatives such as CXL memory pooling, compute-in-memory, or new memory architectures reduce the structural demand for HBM over a 3–5 year horizon?
How will the evolution of HBM affect the balance of power and revenue capture among memory suppliers, advanced packaging providers, and AI chip designers?

sources.title: High Bandwidth Memory for AI
sources.venue: IEEE Symposium on VLSI Technology and Circuits (VLSI Technology and Circuits)
sources.abstract: High-Bandwidth-Memory (HBM) technology is powering the accelerated computing and GPUs behind the AI revolution. This paper discusses the important role HBM architecture, performance, power, capacity, and RAS play in AI hardware. We will compare the HBM memory architecture with more traditional compute memory such as DDR5 focusing on Micron Technology's industry-leading HBM3E. We will end with a look towards the future technology innovations that will be essential to deliver continued HBM scaling.

sources.title: Anisotropic thermal conductivity of high bandwidth memory
sources.abstract: Thermal management of integrated circuits (ICs) is important to prevent thermal hotspots which are the leading cause of IC failure. Thermal management is even more critical in 3D integrated circuits (3D ICs) as the prevalence of thermal hotspots is expected to increase due to the presence of polymers and solder materials that are of low thermal conductivity. Understanding how thermal conductivity is affected by the presence of these materials is required for developing thermally aware IC design. The 3ω method can measure thermal conductivities spanning several orders of magnitude and is appropriate for measuring the thermal properties of layered structures such as 3D ICs. In this work, we use the 3ω method with planar and cylindrical heat flow geometries to determine thermal conductivities of the memory layers and layers with polymer and solder bumps in High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) Random Access Memory (RAM). We determine the in-plane thermal conductivity of the memory layers in HBM as 140 W/m-K, while the through-plane conductivity of the polymer/solder bump layer is 2 W/m-K. Combining the results of x-ray tomography and the 3-omega measurements, we estimate that the effective in-plane thermal conductivity of the overall HBM device is 100 W/m-K while the effective through-plane thermal conductivity is 7 W/m-K. Our results show that the presence of polymers and solder metals results in a significantly decreased through-plane thermal conductivity of a 3D IC compared to a single IC die. Improvement in the thermal performance of 3D ICs will require improvement in the thermal conductivity or the increased contact area of the solder metals used in 3D ICs.

sources.title: Active Interposers for High Bandwidth Memory
sources.venue: International Symposium on Quality Electronic Design (ISQED)
sources.abstract: Integrating the functionality of the base die supporting high bandwidth memory stacks into an active interposer is an effective method to increase physical density while lowering cost. Yield and cost models are presented to compare conventional architectures that use a dedicated base die per stack with configurations that place the necessary logic within a shared active interposer. Yield, latency, and cost comparisons across several technology nodes, interposer areas, and memory stack configurations are discussed. Active interposers with mature technology nodes (e.g., 65 nm) can offer meaningful savings, while more advanced nodes (e.g., 11 nm) are beneficial in configurations composed of multiple memory stacks and smaller area per stack. Memory fetch latencies of passive and active interposers are compared. Integrating base die functionality into an active interposer is shown to be most effective in systems composed of multiple memory stacks and several DRAM layers (e.g., four layers), achieving cost reductions of approximately $20 \%$. The cost advantage diminishes with increasing number of DRAM layers.

sources.title: Effect of non-Fourier heat transport on temperature distribution in High Bandwidth Memory
sources.abstract: High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), as a key development trend in future memory chip technology, significantly enhances computer performance. At the same time, the thermal challenges arising from its stacked architecture have drawn considerable attention. Most existing studies on HBM thermal management are based on Fourier's law, neglecting the non-Fourier effects introduced by the micro/nanoscale structures within HBM. In this study, the Monte Carlo method (MC) is employed to solve the phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) and investigate the impact of non-Fourier heat transport on the thermal behavior of HBM structures. The results reveal that non-Fourier heat transport leads to a junction temperature that is 59.8 K higher than that predicted by Fourier's law. Furthermore, it is found that the phonon transmittance at the chip interlayers has a severe impact on heat dissipation, with the temperature variation reaching up to 56.6 K. These findings provide more accurate thermal insights, which are critical for the optimized design of HBM systems.

sources.title: High-bandwidth prefetcher for high-bandwidth memory
sources.venue: OSTI OAI (U.S. Department of Energy Office of Scientific and Technical Information)
sources.abstract: A method for prefetching data into a cache is provided. The method allocates an outstanding request buffer ("ORB"). The method stores in an address field of the ORB an address and a number of blocks. The method issues prefetch requests for a degree number of blocks starting at the address. When a prefetch response is received for all the prefetch requests, the method adjusts the address of the next block to prefetch and adjusts the number of blocks remaining to be retrieved and then issues prefetch requests for a degree number of blocks starting at the adjusted address. The prefetching pauses when a maximum distance between the reads of the prefetched blocks and the last prefetched block is reached. When a read request for a prefetched block is received, the method resumes prefetching when a resume criterion is satisfied.

sources.title: A 1024 RV-Cores Shared-L1 Cluster with High Bandwidth Memory Link for Low-Latency 6G-SDR
sources.abstract: We introduce an open-source architecture for next-generation Radio-Access Network baseband processing: 1024 latency-tolerant 32-bit RISC-V cores share 4 MiB of L1 memory via an ultra-low latency interconnect (7-11 cycles), a modular Direct Memory Access engine provides an efficient link to a high bandwidth memory, such as HBM2E (98% peak bandwidth at 910GBps). The system achieves leading-edge energy efficiency at sub-ms latency in key 6G baseband processing kernels: Fast Fourier Transform (93 GOPS/W), Beamforming (125 GOPS/W), Channel Estimation (96 GOPS/W), and Linear System Inversion (61 GOPS/W), with only 9% data movement overhead.

sources.title: High Bandwidth Memory: What It Is and Why It Matters
sources.abstract: High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), a specialized type of memory used in most leading artificial intelligence (AI) chips, is a critical enabling technology for AI. HBM is produced at a globally competitive scale by only three companies, and it relies on complex manufacturing processes concentrated in a handful of facilities in East Asia. The authors synthesize technical and market analysis of the HBM ecosystem for researchers and policymakers.

sources.title: On the Thermal Vulnerability of 3D-Stacked High-Bandwidth Memory Architectures
sources.abstract: 3D-stacked High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) architectures provide high-performance memory interactions to address the well-known performance challenge, namely the memory wall. However, these architectures are susceptible to thermal vulnerabilities due to the inherent vertical adjacency that occurs during the manufacturing process of HBM architectures. We anticipate that adversaries may exploit the intense vertical and lateral adjacency to design and develop thermal performance degradation attacks on the memory banks that host data/instructions from victim applications. In such attacks, the adversary manages to inject short and intense heat pulses from vertically and/or laterally adjacent memory banks, creating a convergent thermal wave that maximizes impact and delays the victim application from accessing its data/instructions. As the attacking application does not access any out-of-range memory locations, it can bypass both design-time security tests and the operating system's memory management policies. In other words, since the attack mimics legitimate workloads, it will be challenging to detect.

sources.title: Read Disturbance in High Bandwidth Memory: A Detailed Experimental Study on HBM2 DRAM Chips
sources.abstract: We experimentally demonstrate the effects of read disturbance (RowHammer and RowPress) and uncover the inner workings of undocumented read disturbance defense mechanisms in High Bandwidth Memory (HBM). Detailed characterization of six real HBM2 DRAM chips in two different FPGA boards shows that (1) the read disturbance vulnerability significantly varies between different HBM2 chips and between different components (e.g., 3D-stacked channels) inside a chip, (2) DRAM rows at the end and in the middle of a bank are more resilient to read disturbance, (3) fewer additional activations are sufficient to induce more read disturbance bitflips in a DRAM row if the row exhibits the first bitflip at a relatively high activation count, (4) a modern HBM2 chip implements undocumented read disturbance defenses that track potential aggressor rows based on how many times they are activated. We describe how our findings could be leveraged to develop more powerful read disturbance attacks and more efficient defense mechanisms. We open source all our code and data to facilitate future research at https://github.com/CMU-SAFARI/HBM-Read-Disturbance.

sources.title: 3D Integrated Process and Hybrid Bonding of High Bandwidth Memory (HBM)
Scaling Routers with In-Package Optics and High-Bandwidth Memories
sources.abstract: This paper aims to apply two major scaling transformations from the computing packaging industry to internet routers: the heterogeneous integration of high-bandwidth memories (HBMs) and chiplets, as well as in-package optics. We propose a novel internet router architecture that employs these technologies to achieve a petabit/sec router within a single integrated package. At the top-level, we introduce a novel split-parallel switch architecture that spatially divides (without processing) the incoming fibers and distributes them across smaller independent switches without intermediate OEO conversions or fine-tuned per-packet load-balancing. This passive spatial division enables scaling at the cost of a coarser traffic load balancing. Yet, through extensive evaluations of backbone network traffic, we demonstrate that differences with fine-tuned approaches are small. In addition, we propose a novel HBM-based shared-memory architecture for the implementation of the smaller independent switches, and we introduce a novel parallel frame interleaving algorithm that packs traffic into frames so that HBM banks are accessed at peak HBM data rates in a cyclical interleaving manner. We further discuss why these new technologies represent a paradigm shift in the design of future internet routers. Finally, we emphasize that power consumption may constitute the primary bottleneck to scaling.

sources.title: Characterising CPU-initiated High Bandwidth Memory Access
sources.abstract: Abstract An increasing number of high-performance computers are equipped with high bandwidth memory. Their CPUs have cache-coherent access to this memory type over high-speed interconnects or as unified memory. We analyse two such systems, NVIDIA’s GH200 and AMD’s MI300A. We discuss their memory setup and measure memory access latency and throughput. We evaluate weighted memory page interleaving and strided memory access as candidates for increasing the measured throughput. Weighted interleaving utilises CPU and GPU memory simultaneously and enables exceeding the measured throughput on only CPU or GPU memory for all tested workloads. Using strided memory access, which accesses memory at fixed intervals, we achieve higher throughput than using a non-strided sequential pattern.

sources.title: eBeam process control for yield and reliability in advanced HBM hybrid bonding
sources.venue: Metrology, Inspection, and Process Control XXXVI
sources.abstract: The exponential growth of AI workloads has exposed a critical bottleneck in modern computing architectures, commonly referred to as the AI memory wall. As models scale in complexity and data throughput demands increase, traditional memory hierarchies struggle to deliver the higher bandwidth and lower latency required for efficient AI acceleration. This challenge has elevated High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) as a pivotal solution, offering stacked DRAM with wide input/output (I/O) and proximity to compute units, thereby significantly improving memory access speeds. Compared to conventional Double Data Rate (DDR) memory, HBM provides higher bandwidth per watt, lower latency, and a smaller footprint, making it ideal for AI and high-performance computing (HPC) systems. Its architecture, based on vertically stacked DRAM dies connected via Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs) and micro-bumps enables ultra-wide I/O interfaces that reduce the memory bottleneck in data-intensive applications. To fully realize the potential of HBM in next-generation AI systems, the industry is turning to Hybrid Copper Bonding (HCB) as a key enabler. Both die-to-wafer (D2W) and wafer-to-wafer (W2W), are now the preferred interconnect methods for next-generation HBM stacks. HCB allows fine-pitch, low-resistance interconnects and thermally stable stacking, which are essential for scaling HBM integration beyond the limitations of traditional micro-bump-based packaging. By combining Cu-Cu bonding with dielectric adhesion, HCB supports the mechanical and electrical demands of advanced memory architectures, paving the way for more efficient and scalable AI hardware. As HBM adoption accelerates in AI computing systems, Thermal Compression Bonding (TCB) is reaching its limits in scalability and performance as AI workloads continue to grow AI demands especially in high performance applications. HCB is emerging as the next-generation solution, enabling fine-pitch interconnects down to 8μm today and targeting sub-micrometer pitches in W2W and future D2W applications. However, HCB introduces ’Front-end’-like process requirements with higher complexity and higher cost that drives new process and defect control for HBM [3]. As HBM HCB technologies advance, inline metrology and defect inspection become indispensable to ensure yield and reliability in cost-sensitive advanced packaging environments. Traditional optical metrology and defect review tools are no longer sufficient for process control and defect characterization at sub-micrometer scales. Electron-beam-based solutions, critical-dimension SEM (CD-SEM) and defect-review SEM (DR-SEM), have become essential complementary methods to optical techniques, to provide the nanometer measurements and high-accuracy defect characterization needed to enable fast root-cause analysis and to safeguard yield and reliability in Advanced Packaging manufacturing flows. In this work, we present HBM HCB test cases demonstrating the role of inline critical dimension metrology and defect-review SEM in identifying process excursions and ensuring high-yield manufacturability. In addition, we provide via-level electrical and mechanical performance simulations that illustrate how these eBeam metrology and defect review solutions protect performance and reliability in next-generation AI memory architectures. These test cases were performed on high thickness high warpage wafers, which are typical in advanced packaging processes, while running on inline SEM systems.

sources.title: TSV Built-In Self-Repair Architecture for Lifespan Reliability Enhancement of HBM
sources.abstract: High-bandwidth memory (HBM) is one of the 3-D stacked memory standards that demonstrate high performance, including high bandwidth, large capacity, and low power consumption. However, despite these advantages, issues related to reliability and yield have imposed limitations on mass production. Various methodologies to enhance the reliability of HBM have been proposed, such as built-in self-repair (BISR) architectures and error correction code algorithms. Nevertheless, ensuring the reliability of through-silicon vias (TSV) remains a challenging problem. Existing built-in architectures aiming to enhance TSV reliability often incur significant hardware overhead, limiting practical applications. In this article, an innovative TSV BISR architecture that can detect and repair permanent TSV faults in real time at the user stage is proposed. The proposed architecture significantly enhances the reliability of HBM while implementing it with minimal hardware overhead. Furthermore, it effectively identifies both temporary errors and permanent TSV faults, enabling efficient TSV repairs. Through fast and accurate TSV fault repair, the proposed architecture substantially improves the reliability of HBM.

sources.title: Marvell custom HBM routing and signal integrity analysis
sources.venue: IEEE Electronic Components and Technology Conference (ECTC)
sources.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads scale, high bandwidth memory (HBM) interfaces are increasingly constrained by package interconnect limitations rather than DRAM capability. Conventional JEDEC HBM architectures rely on wide, standardized PHY interfaces that impose rigid pad pitch, breakout topology, and beachfront depth, resulting in long interposer channels, high routing density, large PHY area consumption on the main ASIC die, and rapidly increasing metal layer counts. At advanced data rates, these PHY-driven constraints exacerbate insertion loss, crosstalk, and manufacturability challenges, limiting sustainable bandwidth scaling.This paper presents Marvell’s custom HBM (cHBM) architecture that replaces the standard JEDEC PHY with a high-density die-to-die (D2D) interface implemented on a custom logic base die within the HBM stack. In addition to shortening interposer channels, this approach eliminates the JEDEC PHY and controller area on the main ASIC die, enabling higher logic density for compute and accelerators, while simultaneously enabling custom memory-side functionality to be integrated into the HBM base die. Unlike prior HBM work focused on memory device scaling or aggregate system bandwidth, this study quantifies interposer routing, channel length, and signal-integrity (SI) behavior and compares cHBM directly with JEDEC-based HBM across multiple interposer technologies.The proposed cHBM architecture reduces interface beachfront depth from 3.3 mm to 1.1 mm (~67%), shortening the channel length while maintaining identical line width/spacing (2 µm/2 µm) and routing layer count. Full-wave simulations show CHBM insertion loss below −1.28 dB and return loss better than −15 dB at 16 GHz, with near-end and far-end crosstalk below −30 dB. Time-domain analysis at 32 Gbps bidirectional operation yields eye openings of 0.278 V/0.75 UI (FEXT) and 0.269 V/0.72 UI (NEXT), exceeding die-to-die requirements.The design achieves 32.8 Tbps (4.1 TB/s) using 1024 channels at 32 Gbps, equivalent to a 2048-bit JEDEC interface at 16 Gbps, without doubling interface width or main-die PHY area. These results demonstrate that custom PHY and packaging co-optimization enables scalable bandwidth growth, improved area efficiency, and enhanced integration flexibility within practical electrical and manufacturable limits

sources.title: A Development of a Robust Computer Vision-based Framework for Metrology and Inspection of Stacked Die in HBM Process
sources.venue: JSTS Journal of Semiconductor Technology and Science
sources.abstract: The rapid advancement of high bandwidth memory (HBM) technology introduces significant challenges in metrology due to its complex 3D stacked die architecture. Conventional measurement and inspection tools, optimized for planar DRAM wafers, fail to accurately assess critical die-to-die alignment parameters such as die shift and tilt, particularly post-bonding. This paper presents a novel metrology methodology leveraging infrared (IR) imaging combined with advanced image processing algorithms to overcome these limitations. A dual-scan system captures both base wafer fiducials and top die patterns, enabling precise alignment measurement within stacked HBM assemblies. Edge enhancement using Sobel filtering and normalized cross-correlation (NCC) techniques facilitate robust pattern recognition and sub-pixel alignment, addressing challenges posed by low contrast and IR resolution constraints. Experimental validation on production-grade HBM wafers demonstrates superior recognition rates and measurement repeatability, establishing the proposed approach as a reliable and efficient solution for next-generation semiconductor metrology. The integration of IR optics and sophisticated algorithmic processing significantly improves inspection coverage, contributing to enhanced yield and manufacturing robustness in advanced 3D memory technologies.

sources.title: Development of Embedded Bridge Die Interposer Using Fan-Out Packaging for Heterogeneous Integration of NPUS and HBMS
sources.abstract: The increasing demands of high-performance computing (HPC) and artificial intelligence (AI) systems have intensified the need for advanced heterogeneous integration of neural processing units (NPUs) and high-bandwidth memories (HBMs) within compact, high-density packages. Conventional silicon interposer technology, constrained by 300 mm wafer size and associated yield and cost limitations, poses significant challenges for scalable system-in-package (SiP) designs. In this work, nepes presents a novel Embedded Bridge Die Interposer architecture utilizing fan-out wafer-level packaging (FOWLP) to overcome these limitations. The proposed solution integrates three NPUs and six HBM stacks interconnected via embedded silicon bridges, supporting UCIe-compliant 45μm bump pitch for NPU-to-NPU links and 73μm bump pitch for HBM-to-NPU interfaces. Encapsulation within the fan-out structure enables efficient signal and power redistribution through fine-line redistribution layer (RDLs), while a co-developed Cu Post structure enhances vertical power delivery and thermal performance. Comprehensive process developmentencompassing precise die placement, molding, RDL formation, and dual-pitch bumping-has established a robust and scalable manufacturing flow. Additionally, parallel development of 600 mm × 600 mm panel-level-packaging (PLP) demonstrates scalability beyond wafer-level constraints. This work establishes fan-out Embedded Bridge Interposer technology as a high-performance, cost-effective, and scalable alternative for nextgeneration chiplet-based AI and HPC systems

sources.title: Rethinking memory hierarchy policies in DRAM+HBM systems
sources.abstract: Efficient management of heterogeneous memory systems integrating high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is critical for overall performance. Conventional approaches often assume that dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) is the fastest tier, which may not hold true in HBM-equipped configurations. This study aimed to evaluate the performance impact of reconfiguring memory hierarchy policies by shifting the preference from DRAM to HBM in DRAM+HBM systems. The research employed a modified Ambix framework, adapting migration policies to designate HBM as the fast tier and tuning internal parameters to better suit the DRAM+HBM architecture. Performance was assessed using HPCG and AMG benchmarks on a dual-socket server. It was established that placing all data in HBM yielded performance gains of up to 24% over DRAM-only execution. The analysis demonstrated that standard Linux NUMA balancing could cause up to 4% performance degradation because it incorrectly promoted memory pages to the slower DRAM tier. Investigations revealed that while default Ambix configurations might reduce performance by up to 23%, favouring HBM improved results by 1.4% to 22% over DRAM-preferred policies. Furthermore, internal parameters were tuned to reduce page table scanning frequency and increase migration limits per cycle. These modifications achieved a 3-7% performance gain for the HPCG benchmark compared to the baseline system. For the AMG benchmark, experimental results showed variations from 1.5% degradation to 1.4% improvement, depending on the DRAM:HBM capacity ratios. These findings can enable system architects to optimise memory tiering in next-generation servers without requiring kernel or application modification

sources.title: Assembly Technology for FO-MCM with HBM in HPC Application
sources.abstract: As the industry moves forward the age of more than Moore, the next generation of packaging moves forward high density of chiplet or die splitting package integration. Especially for high performance computing applications, the advance packaging is to provide the economic benefits to integrate multiple chiplet dies by silicon or organic interposer. Organic interposer is one of the alternative interface for die to die interconnection. It is well-known by FO-MCM to apply in chiplets integration and ASIC to Serdes dies integration by the homogeneous package integration concept. Due to the motivation of AI computing and HPC market growth, the trend is formed to integrate the packaged HBM into packaging module as the heterogeneous integration package (HIP). Both of the platforms, 2.5D with silicon interposer base and FO-EB with partial bridge die as interconnection media, have already launched to market in recent years. FO-MCM with purely organic interposer, is also discussed to implement into the heterogeneous integration field. The fully organic interposer can provide the flexible design in multiple RDL layers and line / space for HPC products. In this study, it is to address FO-MCM platform with purely organic interposer to implement heterogeneous packaging with integrated HBMs. Chip last approach in FO-MCM has the advantage to control RDL quality and take “known-good RDL” for top die cost rescuing. The fan-out RDL configuration is 4 layers with min, L/S of 2/2um. In the verification processes, based on the simulation analysis, the warpage and stress are optimized by material and under-fill selections in this discussion. The assembly results indicated the warpage and reliability validation passed by MSL4, TCT700x, uHAST96, and HTST1000hrs conditions.

sources.title: ScalaBFS2: A High-performance BFS Accelerator on an HBM-enhanced FPGA Chip
sources.venue: ACM Transactions on Reconfigurable Technology and Systems
sources.abstract: The introduction of High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) to the FPGA chip makes it possible for an FPGA-based accelerator to leverage the huge memory bandwidth of HBM to improve its performance when implementing a specific algorithm, which is especially true for the Breadth-First Search (BFS) algorithm that demands a high bandwidth for accessing the graph data stored in memory. Different from traditional FPGA-DRAM platforms where memory bandwidth is the precious resource due to the limited DRAM channels, FPGA chips equipped with HBM have much higher memory bandwidths provided by the large quantities of HBM channels, but still a limited amount of logic (LUT, FF, and BRAM/URAM) resources. Therefore, the key to design a high-performance BFS accelerator on an HBM-enhanced FPGA chip is to efficiently use the logic resources to build as many as possible Processing Elements (PEs) and configure them flexibly to obtain as high as possible effective memory bandwidth that is useful to the algorithm from the HBM, rather than partially emphasizing the absolute memory bandwidth. To exploit as high as possible effective bandwidth from the HBM, ScalaBFS2 conducts BFS in graphs in a vertex-centric manner and proposes designs, including the independent module (HBM Reader) for memory accessing, multi-layer crossbar, and PEs that implement hybrid mode (i.e., capable of working in both push and pull modes) algorithm processing, to utilize the FPGA logic resources efficiently. Consequently, ScalaBFS2 is able to build up to 128 PEs on the XCU280 FPGA chip (produced with the 16 nm process and configured with two HBM2 stacks) of a Xilinx Alveo U280 board and achieves performance of 56.92 Giga Traversed Edges Per Second (GTEPS) by fully using its 32 HBM memory channels. Compared with the state-of-the-art graph processing system (i.e., ReGraph) built on top of the same board, ScalaBFS2 achieves 2.52x~4.40x performance speedups. Moreover, when compared with Gunrock running on an Nvidia A100 GPU that is produced with the 7 nm process and configured with five HBM2e stacks, ScalaBFS2 achieves 1.34x~2.40x speedups on absolute performance, and 7.35x~13.18x speedups on power efficiency.

sources.title: Si Characterization on Thinning and Singulation Processes for 2.5/3D HBM Package Integration
sources.abstract: As stacking technologies, such as 2.5D and 3D packages, continue to accelerate in advanced semiconductor components, the singulation and thinning of Si wafers are becoming increasingly critical. Despite their importance in producing thinner and more reliable Si chips, achieving high reliability remains a challenge, and comprehensive research on the effects of these processing techniques on Si chip integrity is lacking. In this study, the impacts of wafer thinning and singulation on the fracture strength of Si wafers were systematically compared. Three different grinding processes, namely fine grinding, poly-grinding, and polishing, were used for thinning, and the resulting surface morphology and roughness were analyzed using scanning electron microscopy and an interferometer. In addition, the residual mechanical stress on the wafer surface was measured using Raman spectroscopy. The fracture strength of Si wafers and chips was assessed through three-point bending tests. Singulation, including blade dicing, laser dicing, and stealth dicing, was evaluated for its impact on fracture strength. Among these processes, polishing for wafer thinning exhibited the lowest full-width half maximum and intensity ratio of Raman shifts (I480/I520), indicating minimal residual stress and surface defects. Consequently, Si wafers and chips processed through polishing demonstrated the highest fracture strength. Moreover, the 60 µm thick Si wafers and chips showed the highest fracture strength compared with those with thicknesses of 90 and 120 µm, possibly because of the increased flexibility, which mitigates stress. Among the singulation methods, stealth dicing yielded the highest fracture strength, outperforming blade and laser dicing. The combination of wafer thinning via polishing and singulation via stealth dicing presents an optimal solution for producing highly reliable Si chips for 2.5D and 3D packaging. These findings may be valuable in selecting optimal processing technologies for high-reliability Si chip production in industrial settings.

sources.title: Analysis of Disease Prevention Behavior Based on Health Belief Model (HBM)
sources.venue: Public Health and Safety International Journal
sources.abstract: Disease prevention behavior is an essential component of public health promotion, yet its psychological determinants require further exploration in the post-COVID-19 Malaysian context. This study analyzes factors influencing disease prevention behavior using the Health Belief Model (HBM) framework. A quantitative cross-sectional approach was applied to 320 respondents from Malaysian urban communities through purposive sampling. Analysis was conducted using SEM-PLS (SmartPLS 4.0) with 5,000 bootstrapping subsamples. Results demonstrate that self-efficacy (β=0.358, p<0.001), perceived benefits (β=0.319, p<0.001), perceived susceptibility (β=0.287, p<0.01), perceived severity (β=0.241, p<0.01), and perceived barriers (β=-0.196, p<0.05) significantly influence disease prevention behavior. Cues to action moderated the perceived susceptibility–prevention behavior relationship (β=0.143, p<0.05). The model explained 61.7% of variance (R²=0.617, Q²=0.389). Findings support individually-tailored health promotion interventions and community self-efficacy strengthening.

sources.title: Folded Banks: 3D-Stacked HBM Design for Fine-Grained Random-Access Bandwidth
sources.venue: Proceedings - International Symposium on Computer Architecture/Proceedings
sources.abstract: Despite significant improvements in peak bandwidth, the HBM industry has neglected random-access (irregular) bandwidth, limiting performance in many real-world applications.Improving effective HBM bandwidth is challenging due to power-constrained activations and coarse-grained, long-distance data movement.Rather than addressing these issues directly, hardware vendors have opted for incremental changes, achieving a 6.4× increase in sequential access bandwidth over two generations while leaving the irregular bandwidth challenges unresolved.To remedy this, we introduce Folded Banks (FB-HBM), a novel 3D bank design that redistributes bank subarrays ("folds") across multiple dies and relocates command, control, and global sense amplifiers to an additional base layer.By implementing this logic in a new base layer, we eliminate the DRAM die overheads inherent in previous designs.This architecture enables vertical routing of intra-bank wires-column select lines (CSLs) and master data lines (MDLs)-through thin-pitch through-silicon vias (TSVs) and hybrid bonds, significantly reducing RC power losses.By employing self-timed sense amplifiers, we eliminate costly dummy subarrays * Work done while Wantong Li was an intern at AMD RAD.

findings.claim: Reliability and yield problems in stacked HBM, notably through-silicon via (TSV) faults, are described as limiting mass production. The proposed repair architecture is only claimed, with no quantified results in the abstract.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The abstract states the limitation and says existing TSV repair schemes carry significant hardware overhead. The proposed fix is asserted without numbers in the abstract, so its real-world effectiveness is a gap. One abstract supports this.
findings.supporting_excerpt: issues related to reliability and yield have imposed limitations on mass production

findings.claim: Metrology for bonded HBM stacks is a manufacturing bottleneck: tools built for planar DRAM reportedly cannot measure post-bonding die shift and tilt, so new IR/image-processing methods are needed. Hybrid-bonding process control is also being framed as a yield and reliability issue.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The quote comes from the computer-vision paper. The eBeam paper's title points to yield and reliability control needs in hybrid bonding, but its abstract is truncated and reports no defect data. The proposed metrology is validated on production-grade wafers, but the abstract gives no figures, so the improvement cannot be gauged.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Conventional measurement and inspection tools, optimized for planar DRAM wafers, fail to accurately assess critical die-to-die alignment parameters such as die shift and tilt, particularly post-bonding.

findings.claim: HBM bandwidth scaling is increasingly limited by package interconnect (PHY, interposer routing, signal integrity) rather than by the DRAM itself. A vendor-specific custom HBM base die is proposed as the remedy, which departs from the JEDEC standard and could fragment the ecosystem.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The quoted constraint is the authors' own framing in a vendor paper. The fragmentation risk is my inference: custom base dies imply bespoke co-design with the memory vendor and the ASIC vendor. The abstract is truncated before the quantified results, so the size of the benefit is unseen.
findings.supporting_excerpt: high bandwidth memory (HBM) interfaces are increasingly constrained by package interconnect limitations rather than DRAM capability

findings.claim: Headline HBM bandwidth gains are mostly for sequential access. Authors argue random-access bandwidth has been neglected, and that effective bandwidth on real workloads depends on logic resources and design effort. Peak figures may therefore overstate useful bandwidth for irregular workloads.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The quote is the authors' claim, and the paper proposes its own alternative design, so the framing is not neutral. The abstract does not show whether the evidence is simulation-based. ScalaBFS2 separately stresses effective over absolute bandwidth on HBM FPGAs, which is consistent but indirect. Both are single-paper, workload-specific findings.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Despite significant improvements in peak bandwidth, the HBM industry has neglected random-access (irregular) bandwidth, limiting performance in many real-world applications.

findings.claim: Silicon-interposer 2.5D integration of HBM faces cost and yield limits, and several alternatives (fan-out embedded bridge, panel-level, purely organic interposers) are being developed. Dependence on silicon interposers is therefore not settled, and the alternatives have unproven maturity.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The nepes abstract states silicon interposers are constrained by 300 mm wafer size and associated yield and cost limitations. It claims a robust, scalable flow but reports no yield, thermal or reliability data in the abstract. The 600x600 mm panel work is described only as 'demonstrating scalability'. Both papers are conference or proceedings papers that may not be fully peer reviewed. Absence of yield data is a gap, not proof of failure.

findings.claim: Wafer thinning and singulation, needed for HBM die stacks, affect chip fracture strength. The authors say comprehensive research on how these processes affect chip integrity is lacking.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The paper compares grinding, polishing and dicing methods and finds polishing gives the highest fracture strength. This indicates that process choice matters for mechanical reliability. The abstract does not give HBM-stack-level failure data.
findings.supporting_excerpt: achieving high reliability remains a challenge, and comprehensive research on the effects of these processing techniques on Si chip integrity is lacking

findings.claim: System-level HBM benefits depend on software policy and workload. Default memory-tiering and NUMA behaviour can lower performance on HBM+DRAM systems, and tuned results varied from small degradation to gains depending on benchmark.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: Evidence is narrow: two HPC benchmarks (HPCG, AMG) on one dual-socket server. The abstract also reports gains of up to 24% over DRAM-only execution, which is modest relative to peak-bandwidth marketing figures. It is not an AI workload and the abstract is truncated for AMG results.
findings.supporting_excerpt: standard Linux NUMA balancing could cause up to 4% performance degradation because it incorrectly promoted memory pages to the slower DRAM tier

hype_flags: 'Hybrid copper bonding is now the preferred interconnect for next-generation HBM': stated in a process-control paper whose abstract is truncated and reports no yield or defect data.
'Robust and scalable manufacturing flow' for fan-out embedded bridge and panel-level packaging: vendor self-assessment with no yield, thermal or reliability numbers in the abstract.
Peak or sequential HBM bandwidth multiples (e.g., 6.4x over two generations): authors argue irregular-access bandwidth is unresolved, so effective gains are workload dependent.
'Proposed architecture substantially improves reliability' (TSV repair): no quantified results in the abstract.

finding.claim: S1 treats a RAND book blurb (src_a6f57ff013) and a Micron-authored conference paper (src_013823ba92) as verified facts about market structure and manufacturing geography. The abstracts only assert 'three companies' and 'East Asia'. They give no data, and the Micron paper is a vendor perspective. The 'most leading AI chips' wording is also loose.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The quote shows the claim is an assertion in a summary abstract. The finding repeats it as verified without supporting numbers. Supply concentration is plausible but unquantified in the evidence available.
finding.supporting_excerpt: HBM is produced at a globally competitive scale by only three companies, and it relies on complex manufacturing processes concentrated in a handful of facilities in East Asia.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S2 describes HBM3E as 'industry-leading' and future innovation as 'essential'. That is the vendor's own framing (Micron) in a single abstract, not independent evidence. The abstract gives no roadmap, no specific innovations, no performance figures. 'Suppliers are working on scaling' generalizes from one company's paper.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The claim is marketing language by an interested party, so it should not be labelled verified_fact about the industry. It is one company's self-description.
finding.supporting_excerpt: focusing on Micron Technology's industry-leading HBM3E. We will end with a look towards the future technology innovations that will be essential to deliver continued HBM scaling.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S3 and S4 present thermal conclusions as settled, but they rest on two arXiv preprints. S3 is a measurement of one device's effective conductivity, which cannot be generalized across HBM generations or vendors. S4 is a Monte Carlo phonon BTE simulation only. The 59.8 K junction-temperature excess depends on assumed structures and interlayer phonon transmittance, and the abstract shows no experimental validation or real-workload power. 'Substantially higher' risks being read as a real-device result.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The evidence is simulation-only (S4) and a single-sample measurement (S3), both unreviewed preprints. The labels should be tempered, with the results flagged as model-dependent.
finding.supporting_excerpt: the Monte Carlo method (MC) is employed to solve the phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) and investigate the impact of non-Fourier heat transport on the thermal behavior of HBM structures.

finding.claim: S5 states a thermal attack on HBM as a researched vulnerability and labels it verified_fact. The source only 'anticipates' such attacks. The abstract reports no demonstration, no measured effect size and no feasibility analysis on real hardware. The claim that such attacks evade detection is also a conjecture. This is a speculative threat model from one preprint.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The word 'anticipate' marks a hypothesis. S12's 'converging concern' builds on this and on two physics preprints that never address security, so the convergence is the agent's own synthesis resting on a single speculative paper.
finding.supporting_excerpt: We anticipate that adversaries may exploit the intense vertical and lateral adjacency to design and develop thermal performance degradation attacks
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S6 is accurate as stated, but it omits the abstract's own caveat that the characterization covers six HBM2 chips on FPGA boards. HBM2 is an older generation, and the sample is small. Defence mechanisms and vulnerability in HBM3/HBM3E are not covered, so the finding should not be read as describing current HBM.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The sample size and generation limit generalization to the HBM3E parts that dominate AI chips.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Detailed characterization of six real HBM2 DRAM chips in two different FPGA boards shows that (1) the read disturbance vulnerability significantly varies between different HBM2 chips
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S7 reports the active-interposer cost benefit without its conditions. The roughly 20% saving is a yield-and-cost model result (not a fabricated or measured system), applies only to multi-stack, several-layer configurations, and shrinks as DRAM layer count rises. Current HBM trends toward taller stacks (more layers) work against it. The paper's own caveats mean the finding says little about real adoption.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The evidence is a model-based estimate under assumptions about nodes and yields, with no fabricated or measured silicon in the abstract. 'Claimed' in S7 is appropriate, but the label verified_fact overstates.
finding.supporting_excerpt: achieving cost reductions of approximately $20 \%$. The cost advantage diminishes with increasing number of DRAM layers.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S8, S9 and S10 are presented as evidence of HBM spreading into new domains, but each is a niche, early-stage item. S8 is an architectural proposal evaluated on traffic traces, and the abstract says power may be the primary bottleneck. S10 is a RISC-V research architecture using HBM2E as a link, not a deployed 6G system. S9 is a measurement on two specific APU/superchip systems. None shows market traction, and the S9 'strided access outperforms sequential' result is likely platform-specific.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: These are proof-of-concept or characterization papers. Presenting them as verified HBM trends overstates their significance, and S8's own abstract flags a major unresolved constraint the finding omits.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Finally, we emphasize that power consumption may constitute the primary bottleneck to scaling.

finding.claim: S11's claim that research momentum is 'concentrating less on raw bandwidth' is unsupported. It is inferred from a handful of papers selected by search, with no count, baseline or bibliometric comparison. The retrieved set also includes bandwidth-focused work (e.g., Folded Banks, custom HBM) that is not weighed. It is also contradicted by the possibility that retrieval simply surfaced thermal and security papers. Combined with the S1/S2 sources, it adds a selection-bias risk.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: A trend claim needs systematic sampling. Eight hand-picked, mostly low-citation papers cannot show a shift in research emphasis, and the cited papers include some about bandwidth itself.

finding.claim: The findings omit manufacturing, yield and reliability risks (TSV faults, hybrid-bonding process control, metrology gaps, thinning/singulation fracture strength) that bear on whether HBM supply can scale. Together with the concentrated supply in S1, these are the main supply-side risk and are missing.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The quote supports the yield limitation. The metrology and thinning papers add that new inspection methods and further research on chip integrity are needed.
finding.supporting_excerpt: issues related to reliability and yield have imposed limitations on mass production.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: The findings quote peak or best-case bandwidth (S10's 98% of 910 GB/s, S9's throughput gains) without the caveat that effective bandwidth depends on access pattern and software. Irregular workloads see little of the gains from sequential-bandwidth scaling, and default tiering can degrade performance.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The quote is from the Folded Banks paper. The tiering paper reports that standard NUMA balancing can cause up to 4% degradation, so system-level gains are conditional.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Despite significant improvements in peak bandwidth, the HBM industry has neglected random-access (irregular) bandwidth, limiting performance in many real-world applications.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

limitations: Abstracts only (one is metadata only, one truncated mid-sentence); no full-paper methods, data or error bars were seen.
Only 12 papers, and one (Health Belief Model, src_d343eb35a5) is off-topic. src_4085e09b25 has no abstract and was not used.

The set contains no papers on thermal limits, power delivery, supply concentration, HBM pricing or capacity, or competing memory technologies, so those risks are unassessed. This is a gap, not evidence of no problem.

Many sources are vendor or conference papers (Marvell, nepes, AMD-affiliated) with an interest in the solutions they present; all are from OpenAlex, and peer-review status for conference items is unclear.
The papers are largely engineering proposals, so counter-evidence on whether these risks have actually been resolved in volume production is not covered.
Only titles and abstracts were reviewed. Some abstracts are truncated, and two sources have metadata only (src_c0ff6f4aa8, src_4085e09b25).
The evidence set is small and skewed toward recent, low-citation papers and arXiv preprints, so I could not check results against independent replication.
No market, supply or vendor-roadmap data was available, so S1/S2 could be neither confirmed nor refuted beyond noting their provenance.
One retrieved item (src_d343eb35a5, Health Belief Model) is unrelated to high bandwidth memory and was ignored.
The challenges are judged only against the abstracts. Full papers may contain caveats or validation that the abstracts omit.

draft.summary: The evidence shows high bandwidth memory (HBM) moving from research into commercial production. Research output is accelerating (167 to 277 works in 2024-2025, and 358 vs 172 year-to-date in 2026) [S11, S1]. Patent publications are also rising (150 in 2024, 264 in 2025, with 2026 undercounted by publication delay) [P5]. Company filings from Micron, KLA, Applied Materials, FormFactor and Veeco describe HBM sales and equipment demand, and social posts claim supply is sold out through 2027 [M1, M3, M4, M8, M9, X1]. The main uncertainties are concentrated supply and manufacturing yield, thermal and reliability limits, and package interconnect constraints [S1, R1, R2, R3]. All five HBM-linked stocks have fallen sharply with high volatility, which adds price risk [T11]. Several Science findings rest on vendor framing, preprints or simulation, and Risk challenges weaken them [C1, C2, C3, C4]. Research and patent counts do not by themselves show commercial success.
draft.plain_summary: High bandwidth memory is a type of stacked computer memory that feeds data quickly to artificial intelligence chips. Company reports and research activity suggest demand is real and growing. The biggest thing that could slow it is that very few companies can make it, and the stacking process is hard to do reliably at scale.
